Genetics is the branch of biology that studies heredity and variation in living organisms. Heredity is the transmission of characteristics (traits) from parents to their offspring through genes, while variation refers to the differences that exist among individuals of the same species. The work of Gregor Mendel, using garden pea plants, laid the foundation of modern genetics, which is why he is called the father of genetics. WAEC often tests Mendel's experiments and his laws of inheritance.

Explain the terms dominant and recessive.

These terms describe how genes (alleles) show up in an organism. A dominant gene is one whose effect is expressed (shows outwardly) even when only one copy is present; it is written with a capital letter, e.g. T for tallness. A recessive gene is one whose effect is hidden when a dominant gene is present, and it only shows when two copies are present; it is written with a small letter, e.g. t for shortness. So a plant with the genes Tt will be tall, because tallness (T) is dominant over shortness (t).

Cross two heterozygous tall pea plants (Tt x Tt). What is the ratio of offspring?

We use a Punnett square for the cross Tt x Tt. Each parent produces gametes T and t. Combining them gives: TT, Tt, Tt, tt. Counting the results: 1 TT (pure tall), 2 Tt (mixed but tall), and 1 tt (short). So the genotype ratio is 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt, and the phenotype ratio is 3 tall : 1 short. This 3:1 ratio is the classic result of a Mendelian monohybrid cross, frequently tested in WAEC.
